title: Characterizing adversarially robust PAC learnability
formal: The historical question asks for a combinatorial complexity measure that characterizes adversarially robust PAC learnability of a binary hypothesis class \(H\) under a fixed perturbation rule \(U\). It is answered by the global one-inclusion dimension \(D_U(H)\) defined below: in the sources’ statistical learning model, \[D_U(H)<\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\text{ is realizably robustly PAC learnable under }U\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad H\text{ is agnostically robustly PAC learnable under }U.\] The learner may be improper and may use full knowledge of both \(H\) and \(U\). This archived record reports the 2022 characterization of the original 2019 question. It retains the original source’s empirical-process measurability convention; it does not assert an extension to arbitrary nonmeasurable classes or certify a fully specified new Lean benchmark.

source_formulation.text: Find a combinatorial complexity measure that is finite exactly when a hypothesis class is adversarially robustly PAC learnable under its specified perturbation rule.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

why: Robust prediction requires correctness on every allowed perturbation of a fresh point, so ordinary statistical dimension can overestimate or misdescribe the task. A characterization identifies exactly which combinations of hypotheses and perturbations admit distribution-free learning, even when efficient computation is not requested.
status_note: Resolved in the source’s statistical model by Montasser–Hanneke–Srebro, NeurIPS 2022: Theorems 5–6 characterize realizable robust learnability by finiteness of the global one-inclusion dimension, and Theorem 9 gives agnostic learnability when that dimension is finite. This answers the 2019 §5 question. The original §2 footnote 1 empirical-process measurability convention is retained; no unrestricted nonmeasurable extension, fully self-contained new Lean benchmark, or existing Lean formalization is asserted.

progress.text: Montasser, Hanneke and Srebro prove finite VC dimension sufficient for improper robust learning and ask for a complexity measure that characterizes robust learnability.
The same authors define the global one-inclusion dimension and establish the realizable characterization in Theorems 5–6 and the agnostic upper bound in Theorem 9.

Matched the historical question against the full graph definition, characterization theorems and agnostic guarantee. Archived the resolution with the original measurability convention explicitly retained.

importance.reason: A general characterization of distribution-free adversarial robustness, including classes of infinite ordinary VC dimension and arbitrary perturbation rules in the source model. It resolves a structural gap between known sufficient and necessary conditions rather than improving one restricted algorithm.

sentences: Robust learning requires a predictor to label every allowed perturbation of a fresh example correctly.
The original question asks for a complexity measure that precisely characterizes which classes are learnable under a fixed perturbation rule.
A NeurIPS 2022 theorem answers it using a dimension defined by orientations of a graph of robustly realizable datasets.
Finiteness of this dimension characterizes both realizable and agnostic learnability when arbitrary improper predictors and full knowledge of the perturbation rule are allowed.
The card is archived with the matching theorem and the original source’s measurability qualification, without claiming an efficient algorithm or a completed Lean proof.

definitions:
Let \(X\) be a nonempty instance domain, \(Y=\{-1,+1\}\), and \(\varnothing\ne H\subseteq Y^X\) a class of total predictors. A fixed known map \(U:X\to2^X\) lists the allowed test-time perturbations of each point. There is no metric, radius, finite-domain, computational, or uniform access-oracle restriction on \(U\). For a predictor \(h\), set \(\ell_U(h,x,y)=\mathbf1\{\exists z\in U(x):h(z)\ne y\}\); the loss is zero if \(U(x)\) is empty. Its robust risk under a labeled-data distribution \(P\) is \(R_U(h;P)=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim P}\ell_U(h,x,y)\). The training sample consists of independent unperturbed draws from \(P\). A deterministic learning rule maps finite labeled sequences to total predictors \(X\to Y\), with no requirement that its output belong to \(H\) and no running-time restriction. For every \(\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1)\), realizable robust PAC learnability requires some finite sample size \(m\) and rule \(A\), depending on \(H,U,\varepsilon,\delta\) but not \(P\), such that for every \(P\) admitting \(h^*\in H\) with \(R_U(h^*;P)=0\), \[\Pr_{S\sim P^m}[R_U(A(S);P)\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta.\] The agnostic version quantifies over every \(P\) and replaces the risk bound by \(R_U(A(S);P)\le\inf_{h\in H}R_U(h;P)+\varepsilon\). The infimum need not be attained. Larger samples can be handled by ignoring excess records. Only sample size is charged; the learner is not restricted to seeing \(U\) on training points.

For each integer \(n\ge1\), define a graph \(G_n=(V_n,E_n)\). Its vertices are the size-\(n\) multisets \(v\) of labeled examples such that one hypothesis \(h\in H\) satisfies \(h(z)=y\) for every occurrence \((x,y)\in v\) and every \(z\in U(x)\). Repetitions are permitted. An edge is a pair \((\{u,v\},z)\) where deleting one record \((x,y)\) from \(v\) and one record \((x',y')\) from \(u\) leaves the same size-\(n-1\) multiset, \(y\ne y'\), and \(z\in U(x)\cap U(x')\). Distinct witnesses \(z\) give distinct edges. An orientation chooses one endpoint \(O(e)\) of each edge. For a finite subgraph \(F\) and \(v\in F\), its adversarial out-degree \(a_F(v,O)\) counts the records in \(v\) that witness at least one incident edge oriented to the other endpoint. A record is counted once even if it witnesses many edges; the count uses the multiset convention of the source. A repeated identical labeled record cannot witness such an edge while another copy remains, since the opposite label and common perturbation would contradict realizability of the other vertex. Set \[D_U(H)=\sup\{n\ge1:\exists\text{ finite }F\subseteq G_n\ \forall O\ \exists v\in V(F),\ a_F(v,O)\ge n/3\},\] with value zero for the empty set and infinity if the set is unbounded. A finite subgraph has finitely many vertices and finitely many selected labeled edges; it need not be induced. This is a combinatorial quantity defined without invoking existence of a learner.

Model boundary: the 2019 source, §2 footnote 1, assumes measurable hypotheses and robust losses and standard restrictions ensuring measurability of the empirical processes used in VC theory. The characterization is recorded with that convention, not with a newly imposed finite/countable domain or an assertion that these restrictions hold automatically. The source does not specify those restrictions as a single self-contained predicate. Choosing explicit measurable spaces and proving the required regularity for the claimed full scope remains an interface obligation for a formalization of this historical theorem.
answer_criterion: A formal treatment of the historical resolution must define the global graph and its dimension and prove both directions of the displayed learnability equivalences, with the measurable-space and empirical-process hypotheses made explicit. A sufficient condition such as finite ordinary VC dimension alone is not a characterization, nor is a necessary dimension bound alone. Proving learnability only for proper output or for a learner with merely local access to perturbations changes the original model. No exact finite-sample formula or efficient algorithm is required by the original question. NeurIPS 2022 Theorems 5–6 establish the realizable characterization and near-matching sample dependence; Theorem 9 supplies the agnostic upper implication. This card is archived on that checked mathematical resolution, not on an asserted Lean proof or on a new conjecture about simpler candidate dimensions.

context_blocks.text: A training example shows its original point and label. At prediction time the learner may receive any point in that original point’s allowed perturbation set. Success requires the same correct label throughout the entire set, and the risk averages this all-perturbations requirement over the unknown data distribution.

The 2019 paper proves that finite VC dimension is sufficient for robust learnability when the output predictor can lie outside the original class. VC dimension counts the largest set of points on which every binary labeling is realized by the class. Finiteness is not necessary here: the perturbation rule can collapse a very rich class to a statistically simple robust task.

The original paper also proposes robust shattering quantities as lower bounds. Its open question is to obtain a necessary-and-sufficient complexity measure, rather than to assume that one of those initial candidates already suffices. The 2022 dimension uses all robustly realizable training multisets and their possible conflicting perturbations.

NeurIPS 2022 Theorem 5 proves that finiteness of \(D_U(H)\) is exactly the realizable learnability criterion. Theorem 6 bounds the required sample size, at fixed sufficiently small failure probability and positive dimension, below by a constant times \(D_U(H)/\varepsilon\) and above by that scale times logarithmic factors. Theorem 9 gives an agnostic upper bound of order \(D_U(H)/\varepsilon^2\), again allowing logarithmic and confidence factors.

The result permits global dependence on the known perturbation rule. The 2022 paper separately proves limitations for learners that only see perturbation sets around the observed training points. Those local-access limitations do not negate the unrestricted statistical characterization. Neither source promises efficient computation of the dimension or learner.

The 2022 paper asks further questions about a simpler full-degree graph dimension and about comparison with ordinary VC dimension. Those are additional targets. Their presence does not leave the original existence-of-a-characterization question unanswered, and this card does not substitute them for the resolved historical question.

The original statistical setup expressly suppresses empirical-process measurability details. This archived record exposes that qualification and preserves it in the resolution status, rather than claiming a theorem about all nonmeasurable set systems.
